The Meaning of Life

A question humanity has pondered for millennia — and the answer is yours to create.

Philosophical Perspectives

Existentialism

Existentialist thinkers like Jean-Paul Sartre and Albert Camus argued that life has no inherent meaning — and that this is liberating, not terrifying. We are born into a universe that doesn't care about us, and from that freedom comes both anxiety and the opportunity to create our own purpose.

"Man is condemned to be free." — Jean-Paul Sartre

Absurdism

Camus compared the human search for meaning to Sisyphus pushing a boulder up a hill, only to watch it roll back down. The struggle itself, he said, is enough to fill a heart with meaning. We must imagine Sisyphus happy.

"The only way to deal with an uninspiring world is to inspire yourself." — Albert Camus

Religious & Spiritual Traditions

Many traditions offer answers: Christianity speaks of loving God and neighbor; Buddhism points to the alleviation of suffering through enlightenment; Islam emphasizes submission to the divine and righteous living; Hinduism explores dharma and liberation from the cycle of rebirth. Each offers a framework for understanding why we are here.

Humanism & Purpose

Secular humanists suggest that meaning is found through human connection, contribution, learning, love, and the pursuit of a better world. We give our lives meaning by the choices we make and the lives we touch.

Aristotle & Eudaimonia

The ancient Greeks, particularly Aristotle, proposed that meaning comes from eudaimonia — flourishing. A life well-lived is one of virtuous action, meaningful relationships, and the cultivation of one's potential.

"Happiness is the meaning and the purpose of life, the whole aim and end of human existence." — Aristotle

Common Threads

Across cultures and centuries, certain themes appear again and again:

  • Connection — Love, friendship, community, belonging
  • Contribution — Making something better for those who come after
  • Growth — Learning, evolving, becoming more fully yourself
